description: Handling clicks, typing, and forms the React way.

screens.body:
In React you write onClick, onChange, onSubmit — camelCase — instead of HTML's lowercase onclick. The value is a function, not a string of code.

So <button onClick={handleClick}> wires your function to the click. Note the curly braces: you're passing real JavaScript.

check.question: How do you handle a click in React?

code.snippet:
// display-only: camelCase events
<button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
<input onChange={handleChange} />
<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>

screens.heading: Events use camelCase

screens.body:
onClick={handleClick} hands React the function to run later. onClick={handleClick()} calls it immediately during render — usually the bug behind 'it runs before I click'.

Need arguments? Wrap it: onClick={() => handleClick(item.id)}. The arrow function waits for the click, then calls with the argument.

options: It calls the function immediately during render
check.question: What's wrong with onClick={handleClick()}?

screens.heading: Pass the function — don't call it
screens.keyPoint: No parentheses = runs on click. Parentheses = runs now.

screens.body:
A controlled input gets its text from state: value={name}. React is the single source of truth — the input shows exactly what state says.

Without value, the input keeps its own text and React can't see it. Controlled = React in charge, always.

options: Its value comes from React state
check.question: What makes an input 'controlled'?

screens.heading: Controlled inputs: React owns the text
screens.keyPoint: Controlled input = value comes from state.

screens.body:
Every keystroke fires onChange with an event object. The new text lives at e.target.value — the input element (target) and its current text (value).

The pattern is always the same: read e.target.value, feed it to the setter, React re-renders with the new text.

check.question: Where is the typed text in an onChange handler?

screens.heading: onChange hands you the typed text

screens.body:
A form's default submit reloads the page — fine in 2005, terrible for an app. Call e.preventDefault() in your onSubmit handler to stay on the page.

Then do whatever the submit means in your app: validate, save to state, call an API.

check.question: How do you stop a form submit from reloading the page?

screens.heading: Forms: stop the reload
screens.keyPoint: preventDefault keeps you on the page.

screens.body:
Give each input a name attribute, then read e.target.name in a shared handler to know which field changed. One function, many inputs.

For a small form you can also just write a tiny handler per input — pick whichever reads clearer.

options: Use the input's name attribute to tell them apart
check.question: How can one handler update several inputs?

screens.heading: One handler can serve many inputs
screens.keyPoint: name + e.target.name = one handler, many fields.

screens.body:
Because the input's text lives in state, the rest of the UI can react to it: disable the button while the field is empty, show a character count, display an error.

This is the payoff of controlled inputs — every pixel can respond to what the user typed.

check.question: How do you disable a button while an input is empty?

screens.heading: Drive the UI from state
screens.keyPoint: State drives every pixel, not just the input.
